title: "Free shipping" and the fuller basket
description: Free delivery thresholds are set just above what you meant to spend. The extra item you add to qualify is rarely free at all.

body.heading: The threshold trick
paragraphs: Suppose shipping costs $5, but delivery is "free" over $35 — and your basket holds $28 of things you actually want. Adding a $7 item to cross the line feels clever. But you have spent $7 to save $5, and you own something you never went shopping for.

The threshold is not generosity; it is a target chosen because most baskets fall just short of it. Retailers know the extra item is usually chosen in a hurry, at full price, from whatever the site suggests.

body.heading: Better responses
paragraphs: Option one: pay the $5 shipping and buy only what you came for. Option two: wait and combine — keep a list of genuinely needed items from that shop until a natural order crosses the threshold on its own.
Option three: check whether the same item is available locally at a fair price. A slightly higher shelf price with no shipping and no filler can be the cheapest honest total.

body.heading: Count the basket, not the delivery
paragraphs: Judge every order by the full amount leaving your account for the things you wanted. "Free shipping" on a padded basket costs more than honest shipping on a lean one, every single time.

Some shops offer free collection from a local store instead. If the store is on a journey you already make, that is genuinely free delivery — the only version of the offer that never asks you to buy anything extra.

takeaway: Never add an item just to reach a free-shipping threshold: compare the total basket cost, and let needed items accumulate until they cross the line naturally.
